title: Searching Algorithms: Finding Needles in Data Haystacks

questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of linear search?
questions.rationale: If the target is last or absent, linear search inspects all n items — O(n) — though it needs no ordering.

questions.question: Binary search requires that the data be:
questions.rationale: Halving only works when comparing with the middle tells you which half can contain the target — that inference needs order.

questions.question: In the worked example, searching 23 in [2 5 8 12 16 23 38 56 72 91] compared with which middles, in order?
questions.rationale: First mid = 16 (discard left), then mid = 56 (discard right), then mid = 23 — found in three comparisons.

questions.question: Roughly how many comparisons does binary search need in the worst case for n = 1,000,000?
questions.rationale: O(log₂ n): 2²⁰ ≈ 1,048,576, so at most 20 halvings — versus a million for linear search.

questions.question: Why is mid = low + (high - low) / 2 safer than mid = (low + high) / 2 in some languages?
options: It avoids integer overflow when low + high exceeds the max integer
questions.rationale: low + high can overflow fixed-width integers; the difference form cannot — a real bug that lived in Java's standard library.

questions.question: A hash table achieves average O(1) lookup by:
options: Computing the storage index directly from the key with a hash function
Storing all values in one list
questions.rationale: The hash function maps key → bucket index, so no comparisons are needed; collisions are handled by chaining or probing.

questions.question: When two different keys hash to the same index, it is called a:
questions.rationale: Collisions are resolved by chaining (list per bucket) or open addressing (probing for the next free slot); a good hash keeps them rare.

questions.question: You need both fast point lookups AND range queries (e.g., 'all keys between 40 and 50'). Which structure fits best?
questions.rationale: Hash tables scatter keys, killing order; sorted structures support ranges naturally alongside O(log n) lookup — which is why databases use B-trees.

questions.question: Interpolation search improves on binary search when:
options: Keys are uniformly distributed — it estimates the target's position
questions.rationale: Like opening a phone book near the 'S' section, it guesses by value distribution, reaching O(log log n) average — but degrades to O(n) on skewed data.

questions.question: 'Binary search on the answer' refers to:
options: Searching for a key equal to log n
Binary-searching a monotonic property's threshold value (e.g., minimum feasible capacity)
questions.rationale: When feasibility is monotonic ('works for x ⇒ works for x+1'), you can binary-search the breakpoint itself — the pattern behind many optimisation problems.
